notes: PDF originals were opened read-only and were not modified.
Extracted text is raw pypdf page text with page markers; no spelling correction, translation, or cleanup was applied.

A page is marked as an OCR candidate when it has fewer than 20 visible extracted characters and contains an embedded image, or image detection is unavailable. This is a conservative heuristic, not OCR output.
Empty pages have no extracted text and no detected embedded images. Some vector-only/scanned content may not be identifiable with this heuristic.
Whitespace token counts are estimates, not model-tokenizer counts. The model tokenizer was not downloaded.
Duplicate detection hashes page text after whitespace normalization and case folding; source text is retained regardless.

1.2 Scientific Attitude
 You have to prepare yourself for acquiring knowledge. How to 
do so? Firstly, you must learn how to doubt. Doubt means systematic 
or logical doubt. Let us consider one example. Suppose, all your family 
members are coming back home in the evening from somewhere. You 
have switched on the light but the light does not turn on. What will you 
do ? Perhaps you will switch the light on and off a few more times. If 
still the light does not turn on then you may try with the nearby switch 
of the fan. Suppose the fan also does not turn on. If that happens,  you 
may think that the problem is there with the electricity supply. Then 
you will look at the nearby houses. If the nearby houses are also in 
darkness, then you may be sure that the electricity is out. You see, how 
you are having doubts systematically. Again, whenever you start to 
doubt systematically, there will be a question. In this case, the question 
is ‘why the light does not turn on’?
 After systematic doubt, you are to  look for proof . There is no 
light in the neighbourhood. This is the proof that there is no electricity.
 Last but not the least, one has to be open-minded i.e. whatever 
you say is the truth – it should not be like that. You should listen to 
others also. You may like somebody, but you should not accept his or 
her bad mannerisms. You must be neutral. No prejudice should prevail.
Thus, you  have a scientific attitude if you

Fig. 1.7 : Health check-up by doctor 
Why do birds fly in sleeping position? In sleeping position, they 
experience less obstruction from wind. This is hypothesis. By hypothesis, 
we mean a guess regarding the cause of an incident. Finally, you are to do  
an experiment and verify whether your hypothesis is correct or wrong. 
In this way you can find out the truth and  such truth is knowledge.
Observation, hypothesis and experiment – these three together 
form the scientific method. For acquiring knowledge, scientific method 
is very essential.
It is not that only the scientists need scientific method. This is 
for all. This is even practiced by people of different walks of life. For 
example, if the tyre of your bicycle is flat, you take it to the person who 
can repair it. Firstly, he inspects and tries to find out why the tyre is flat. 
Then he finds out the hole by doing experiment using water. At last, he 
seals the hole so that no air leaks.
Similarly, whenever you have fever, your parents take you to the 
doctor. Fever occurs due to different diseases. The doctor observes you 
and diagnoses the disease from the symptoms. The doctor then  advices 
blood tests to detect the actual disease.

 Our planet Earth is a wonderful place for organisms to live. You 
certainly know something about living organisms. You see various 
plants, birds, insects and other kinds of animals around you, don’t you? 
All of these are living organisms. The organisms perform life processes 
themselves to remain alive. Have you observed what happens when 
a seed germinates? After germination, doesn’t it become a seedling? 
The seedling grows into a tree, bears flowers and then produces fruits. 
Eventually, it dies at a specific time. What do you understand from it? 
Organisms have a specific life span and it differs from one organism to 
another.
2.1 Biodiversity and its meaning 
 While observing our surrounding, you can see various organisms. 
Have you ever gone for a walk by the river side or hilly areas? Have 
you noticed various trees, birds etc. over there? During your school 
vacations, when you visit the gardens or forests you will see different 
kinds of organisms. Some of them are trees and herbs, which we call 
plants. Forest have different kinds of plants. Various kinds of birds, 
butterflies and animals are also there. The colours of birds are different 
and their tweets are also different. Some birds are big and while others 
are small. Many insects live on the trees. Their structures and colours 
are also different.  
 The wings of butterflies are colourful, aren’t they? In our 
environment, we find many multicoloured, charming butterflies. Insects, 
butterflies, birds live on trees. Animals like snakes also live in the forest.

2.2 Significance of biodiversity
We have a great relationship with the organisms found in our 
surroundings. Do you observe these relationships? Is there any 
relationship between birds and crops? What is the relation of a butterfly 
with flower? You know that birds consume crops as food, while others 
help crops by eating the insects that cause damage to them. Butterflies 
feed on the nectar of flowers and as a result they help in plant reproduction. 
Fruits serve as a primary food source for some animals. Think about a 
large tree! Birds build their nests on these trees to live. Insects on trees 
are eaten by birds. As a result, the number of these organisms remain 
balanced. Some birds eat the fruits of trees. The seeds of the fruit come 
out along with the faeces and fall elsewhere. From these seeds, new 
plants grow. In this way the number of trees increases. Birds thus help 
in the extension of forests in this way. Forests provide shelter to the 
animals. Plants in turn provide food to animals, provide oxygen for 
breathing. Animals release carbon dioxide gas during exhalation. This 
gas is used by plants for synthesis of food.

Some of them are bushes and are comparatively short. These are called

hornbill, hargila, bortokola (lesser adjutant stork) etc. make the park 
very attractive. Large snakes like python are also found in Kaziranga 
National Park. The park is teeming with diverse plants and animals.

1 Activity 2.5:
While visiting a garden haven’t you collected some fallen leaves? 
Observe these leaves carefully. Do you see some lines on the lamina 
of the leaves? These are veins and veinlets of leaf. The arrangements 
of veins and veinlets in a leaf is known as venation. The big vein 
from the base to the apex of the leaf is called the midrib. Leaf veins 
originate from midrib. In some leaves, veins originating from the 
midrib are parallel. This is called parallel venation. Banana leaves 
exhibit this type of venation. Similarly, the veins in the leaves of the 
paddy plant are also arranged parallelly. When you observe a leaf of 
a peepal tree, you will see net like pattern of veins which is called 
reticulate venation.

Can we classify plants on the basis of venation?
The venation of plants like paddy, wheat, maize is parallel. The 
roots of these plants are fibrous. On the other hand plants like rose, 
guava, peepal have reticulate venation in their leaves. These type of 
plants have taproots. 
We have discussed venation pattern and root structure. Let’s do 
another activity.

1 Activity 2.6:
¿	 Find a place with leaf greens and herbs.
¿	 Using a ‘khurpi’, carefully dig out a few saplings of leafy  
 greens and herbs along with their roots. Ensure that, the roots  
 do not get damaged.
¿	 Clean the roots  by washing them with water.
¿	 Observe the structure of the roots. 
While observing, you will see that some plants have one main root 
from which some secondary roots originate. This type of arrangement 
of roots is called taproot system. For example, the roots of china rose 
exhibit this type of roots. On the other hand plants like grass have a 
bunch of thin roots arising from the base of the stem. These type of 
roots are called fibrous roots. The plants with reticulate venation tend 
to have taproot. Whereas plants (like grass) with parallel venation 
have fibrous root.

Based on similar characteristics, that we have already discussed, 
plants can be classified into some groups. Similarly, other characteristics 
can also be considered for the same purpose. You have learnt that the 
main basis of classification is the similarities among the plants. 
As in plants, animals can also be classified by observing some 
similar characteristics. This process is called classification. In case of 
classification of animals, characteristics such as body structure, size, 
body movements, laying of eggs or giving birth to new ones etc. are 
taken into consideration. By considering some common characteristics, 
animals can be grouped into broad categories. Again, some other 
common characteristics of the group could be considered to form small 
groups. Such classification helps to study biodiversity.  
¿	Observe the seeds carefully. Both the seeds have seed coat. 
Gently remove the seed coat.
¿	Observe closely the internal structure of the seeds.
Fig.  2.6 : Monocot and dicot seeds 
Cotyledon
You have observed that the seeds have germinated. There are two 
fleshy parts inside the chickpea seeds. Each part is called cotyledon. 
It stores food for the growth of the germinating sprout. Plants whose 
seeds have two cotyledons are called dicotyledons or dicots. Maize 
seeds contain only one cotyledon. Plants bearing such seeds are called 
monocotyledons or monocots. 
 There is a relationship between leaf venation, root type and seed 
structure in dicot and monocot plants. Dicot plants have reticulate 
venation and a taproot system while monocot plants have parallel 
venation and a fibrous root system.

Dr. Robin Banerjee (1908–2003) was a renowned Indian 
naturalist, documentary film maker and   environmentalist. He 
is commemorated  for his extensive contributions to wildlife 
conservation and education. During a visit to Kaziranga National 
Park sometime in the 1950s, Banerjee fell in love with the wild life 
of Assam and decided to settle down at Golaghat, near Kaziranga.
 His passion for nature led him to produce 32 acclaimed wildlife 
documentaries, including ‘Kaziranga, Wildlife of India’ and Madame 
Pompidou Award wining ‘White Wings in Slow Motion’. He also 
authored numerous books and illustrated children’s literature. A 
recipient of the Padma Shri in 1971, Dr. Banerjee was instrumental in 
raising awareness about the rich biodiversity of Assam, particularly 
Kaziranga National Park. His home  at Golaghat was converted  to 
“Uncle Robin’s Natural History Museum”, showcasing artifacts, 
photographs, and paintings from his extensive career. The museum 
serves as a center for nature education and tourism.  
2.5  Adaptation of animals and plants
Animals use different modes of movement. When you observe, you 
will notice that deers have long legs, fishes have spindle-shaped bodies, 
frogs and toads have long and folded limbs. Do you know why this is so ?
An animal’s body structure is suitable for the environment where 
it lives. The size and shape of the body transforms accordingly. All 
organisms get themselves adjusted to live in their environment. They 
adopt various mechanisms to do so. These mechanisms are called 
adaptation. Have you ever observed fishes in an aquarium? The body 
structure of a fish is suitable to move in water.

Have you ever heard of deserts? The desert environment is dry and  
sandy. During day time it is hot and the nights are very cold. Animals 
like snakes live in burrows during the day time to escape from the heat. 
At night they come out in search of food.
 Deserts have a very limited water supply. Hot deserts are 
characterized by scorching heat during the day and freezing temperatures 
at night. As a result, the animals and plants that thrive there are well-
adapted to survive both in intense heat and cold. 
 Camels in hot deserts have long legs with wide hooves. These 
features help camels walk on sandy terrain without sinking. In contrast, 
camels in cold deserts have shorter legs and are not as tall as their hot 
desert counterparts. The shorter legs make it easier for them to navigate 
the rugged and mountainous terrain of cold deserts.
 In deserts, food is scarce, and so camels store their food in 
their humps. Camels in hot deserts have a single hump, which helps 
them  to survive during  food crisis. In contrast, camels in cold deserts 
have two humps that shrink during late winter when food is limited. 
In addition, camels in cold deserts have long hairs from their head to 
neck, providing insulation against the harsh winters of Ladakh. Camels 
excrete minimal amount of urine, produce dry dung, and do not sweat. 
By conserving water, camels can endure long periods without drinking, 
making them well-suited to the desert environment.

 Rhododendrons are stunning flowering plants with bright 
flowers. To withstand the strong winds on the summits of the mountains, 
rhododendrons in the Nilgiri mountain range are shorter in height and 
have smaller leaves. However, rhododendrons are taller in the Himalayan 
region . Therefore, even plants like rhododendrons may display distinct 
characteristics in various locations to withstand the local conditions.
Rhino conservation of Assam
Assam’s rhino conservation has seen dramatic success despite 
near extinction levels in the past. By 1908, Kaziranga’s rhino 
population had dwindled to just 12. Even after that, Assam has 
achieved remarkable success in conserving the one-horned 
rhinoceros, primarily through the efforts taken up by the concerned 
authority at Kaziranga National Park, the natural home to most 
of the global population of this species. Through anti-poaching 
measures, community involvement, and habitat expansion, the rhino 
population in Assam has grown from 600 in the 1960s to over 4,000 
today. and from 1,500 in the 1980s to over 4,014 today. Initiatives 
like the burning of confiscated rhino horns, Assam’s zero-tolerance 
policy against poaching, making the state a global leader in wildlife 
conservation.

You have already learned about organisms. The place where an 
organism naturally lives, is called habitat of the organism. Organisms 
acquire food from the habitats. They also reproduce in their habitats. 
Salim Ali  (1896–1987), 
widely known as the 
“Birdman of India,” 
travelled extensively 
across India to study the 
diverse bird species of the 
region. He meticulously 
documented their habitats 
and migration patterns, 
identifying areas with rich bird diversity. His efforts led to the 
establishment of conservation measures in significant locations such 
as the Ranganathittu Bird Sanctuary in Mandya, Karnataka and the 
Keoladeo National Park in Bharatpur, Rajasthan. Salim Ali authored 
a historic ten-volume series on the birds of the Indian subcontinent. 
In recognition of his contributions to ornithology and conservation, 
he was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 1958  and Padma Vibhushan 
in 1976.
Organisms living in land are called terrestrial organisms. Their  
habitat is terrestrial habitat. Forests, deserts, mountains are examples 
of terrestrial habitat.Organisms living in water are called aquatic 
organisms. Aquatic organisms live in fresh water or saline water 
habitats. The marine organisms live in saline water habitats. These 
habitats contribute to biodiversity. Some animals, such as frogs can live 
in water as well as on land . These are called amphibians.

patches of forests that vary in 
size and  are found across India.

biodiversity treasures are 
protected by local communities.

Pradesh, Meghalaya, sacred groves play a significant role in 
preserving nature and cultural heritage. Many such sacred forests are 
found in the Dima Hasao and Karbi Anglong districts. In many parts 
of Assam, it is also known as “Than”, while the Dimasa tribe in the 
North Cachar Hills refers them to as “Madaico”. These groves reflect 
the community’s deep-rooted respect for biodiversity and tradition.

Healthy Life3
 We all take food everyday. Food refers to an essential substance 
required for our survival. Food is needed by all living beings but the 
way of taking food is different. Green plants prepare their own food. 
Human beings and other animals depend on plants and animals for their 
food. 
 Why is food important for us ?  Food is one of the basic necessity 
of life. Food provides energy to the body for doing various activities. 
Food protects us from diseases and infections. Food helps in the growth 
and repair of our body. It plays a major role in proper functioning of our 
body.

includes rice, legumes, vegetables, fruits, dairy products etc. What 
are these food items and how do we consume them ? To know about

3.1.2 : How have cooking practices changed over time ?
 Cooking is an art of preparing food by using heat to make it 
palatable and digestible. In India, food habits of different regions are 
different. The food choice as well as its preparation may differ from 
one another. The culinary practices and food habits have changed 
significantly over time. 
 Make groups of three or four from among yourselves. Now ask 
the adult whether there is any difference between food items of past and 
present. Have you ever helped in cooking at your home by any means ? 
Write the name of appliances used in the cooking process at your home 
in your notebook.  
    Earlier cooking was done by using earthen or bronze made 
pots, bronze utensils on small open fire furnance (chulha). Now-a-
days we use modern gas stove, microwave, air fryers for cooking. The 
earthen pots have been  replaced with pressure cookers and modern 
cookwares. Earlier grinding was done manually using sil-batta, stone 
grinder (chakki ) and husking pedal (dheki). Now-a-days we use the 
electrical grinder for grinding. These changes have evolved due to the 
advancement in technology, improvement in transportation and better 
communication.

components are called nutrients. The nutrients contained in our food 
are discussed below :
 One of the major nutrients in our food is the carbohydrate. The 
primary sources of carbohydrate are cereals like rice, wheat, maize, 
millet; fruits like mango, banana, pineapple, grapes; vegetables like

sources and animal sources. Fats from plant sources include nuts such as 
walnut, groundnut, almonds; seeds like pumpkin seed, sunflower seed, 
flax seed, sesame seed etc. Olive, coconut and mustard are also source 
of fats. Some fats obtained from animal sources are ghee, cheese, fish 
etc.

 Vitamins and minerals are required in small quantities. These 
protect us from diseases. So these foods are known as protective food. 
 Besides these nutrients our body needs dietary fibers and water. 
Dietary fibers are also known as roughage. Though it does not provide 
any nutrient to our body but is an essential component of our food. This 
helps our body to eliminate undigested food. Whole grains and pulses, 
potatoes, fresh fruits and vegetables are the main sources of roughage.

It also helps in elimination of some wastes from the body through urine 
and sweat. So it is very important to drink sufficient amount of  water 
regularly.

  If a person does not get sufficient amount of  protein in his/her food

  If the diet is deficient in both carbohydrates and proteins for a

 In ancient times, the sailors often suffered from swollen and 
bleeding gums during long voyages. In 1746, during a voyage, Scottish 
physician James Lind observed that sailors who consumed lemons and 
oranges recovered from these symptoms. The bleeding and swollen 
gums are the symptoms of disease called scurvy.
 From the above case it is noticed that consumption of lemons and 
oranges cures scurvy. Vitamin C is present in citrus fruits like lemon 
and oranges which help in curing scurvy. That means, deficiency of 
Vitamin C causes scurvy. Similarly deficiency of iodine in food causes 
goitre. Consumption of iodised salt also can prevent the disease Goitre.

 The food mile refers to the entire distance that a food (rice or 
any other food/grain) travels from the farm to the plate. It can also 
be expressed as the distance travelled by the food from producer to 
consumer. 
 For any food grain, it is  important to reduce food mile. Reducing 
food mile helps to minimise the cost and pollution during its transport. 
Locally produced food also reduces the food mile. So, we get these 
foods at low cost, causing less environment pollution. It supports local 
farmers and keeps our food fresh and healthy. So try to consume the 
foods locally produced in your area. Write down the name of some 
foods which are produced in your locality. 
Let us learn
Food is wasted by people when left unconsumed by them on their 
plates. If we take as much food as we can consume, it will reduce 
wastage of food. Before wasting, we should always realise the 
efforts and time of the farmers and other community people 
involved to get the food from the farm to our plate.

There is a story about the discovery of magnet. About 4000 years 
ago, there was a shepherd named Magnus in Greece. He always carried 
a wooden stick with him while tending sheep. The wooden stick had an 
iron cap at the rear end. Do you know what happened one day? While 
grazing, the tip of his stick got stuck to a large black rock. He could take 
out the stick only after pulling hard. Why did this happen ? It is sure that 
the stone was attracting the iron cap. In this way people came to know 
about the things that can attract iron. This stone that attracted iron was 
called magnetite or loadstone, after the name of the shepherd. This is 
how the English name magnet was derived.
Magnetite is a magnet which is found in nature. Magnets found 
in nature are called natural magnets or loadstones. On the other hand, 
a substance (such as iron) that is attracted by a magnet can be turned 
into a magnet. Such magnets are called artificial magnets. Artificial 
magnets are used in the lids of pencil boxes, toys, laboratories etc.

You have come to know that magnet have two poles. There may be 
attraction or repulsion between the two poles. Opposite poles of two 
magnets attract each other while like poles repeal each other. Let’s do 
an activity to know more about it.  
       Fig. 4.7 : Attraction and Repulsion of magnet             
       [a] Two bar magnets
(b) N-pole brought closer to N-pole [c] S-pole brought closer to N-pole
 What do you learn from the activity? Firstly, the properties of 
the two poles of a magnet are not the same. Secondly, there is repulsion 
between the same poles (north-north or south-south) of the two magnet.
But the opposite poles attract each other. You can play a game using this 
behaviour. Keep a bar magnet vertically in a small-mouthed bottle. Try 
to put another bar magnet in the mouth of the bottle. Bring the opposite 
poles of the two magnets closer to each other. The magnet inside the 
bottle will come up and stick to the magnet above. On the other hand if 
you bring the same pole, the upper magnet will float in air.
Fig. 4.8 : Attraction and Repulsion of magnet

magnet? Now bring the south pole of the second magnet near to the 
north pole of the first magnet. The two magnets cling together, isn’t it?

So, we can conclude that a freely 
suspended magnet always aligns in 
particular direction. This is the north-
south direction. The end pointing 
towards north is the north pole of the 
magnet and the south pointing end 
is the south pole. Why does a freely 
suspended magnet always aligns north-
south direction ? This is because our 
Earth is like a huge bar magnet. This is 
called geomagnet.

magnet on one end (say, pointed end) of the needle. Then rub the magnet 
over the needle to the other end. Lift the magnet and rub the needle 
from the same end to the other end as before. Rub the needle 30-40
times from the same end. Don’t rub in the opposite direction. Now 
Fig 4.12 : Picture of a 
compass
The south pole of the geomagnet indicates north while its 
north pole indicates south. So now you understand why a freely 
suspended magnet remains in the north-south direction, don’t you?
 Try again the above activity by using an iron rod, wooden or 
plastic scale instead of a magnet. Do they indicate north and south 
direction when they are at rest ? Is such a bar or scale a magnet?
 This property of magnet is used to determine direction on 
the earth’s surface. In ancient times, travellers used natural magnet 
for the purpose. They determined direction by suspending the 
natural magnet with a thread. This property 
of magnet is used to develop a compass.
 A compass is a small box with a glass lid. It 
has a small needle-shaped magnet in the middle. 
This needle can rotate freely. You know that, at 
steady state, the two ends of the magnet always 
point in the north-south direction. The north pole 
of the magnet is marked red. Thus from the needle 
of the compass we find north and south directions. 
This facilitates the determination of the other 
directions (east and west). This is the reason why 
sailors use a compass to ascertain directions at sea.

 A childhood incidence of the world famous 
Physicist Albert Einstein goes like this. When he 
was five years old, one of his relative gifted him a 
compass. Child Einstein observed the compass in 
various ways. He wondered why the magnetic needle 
always keeps pointing north-south direction. What 
type of invisible force is there that keeps the needle in that position. 
He became quite curious and wanted to know the reason. He started 
asking his father and uncle about this. Such questions led him to learn 
about electricity and some other scientific discoveries. A school boy 
gave him some books on mathematics, physics and geometry to read.

to get such a great scientist.

4.3 Use of magnet   
 We use magnets for various purposes. For example, magnet 
is used in various types of toys, doors of cupboards, pencil boxes, 
refrigerators, electric motors, laboratories etc. Magnets are attached 
to the doors of houses and cupboards. As a result, the door doesn’t open 
on its own; it opens only when you pull it. Moreover, magnets are also 
used in some medical devices such as MRI machines. They are also 
used in microphones, speakers etc.

Magnets lose their magnetic properties when heated, hammered or 
dropped from above. They should be kept away from computers, 
television, mobile, cassettes, compact disc (CD), transistors etc to 
preserve magnetism.
4.4 Preserving magnet  
  A magnet should not be kept open. If the poles of a magnet are left 
open for several days, the magnetism gradually decreases. In case of bar 
magnets, the opposite poles of two or more magnets should be placed 
in the same direction. The magnets should be separated by a piece of 
wood. Each end of the array of magnets should be joined by soft iron. 
In the case of horseshoe magnet, a piece of iron should be kept attached 
to each pole.

What are the things that you bring with you to the school? You bring 
books, notebooks, pen, pencil, eraser, etc. right? In your classroom also 
there are certain objects like chairs, tables, chalk, duster, desk-bench. 
You also have many things in your house. These include food items, 
clothes, utensils, cooking gas, chairs, tables, beds etc. There are also 
many things around the house and the school. 
Definitely the colour and shape of all the objects are not the same. 
Do you feel the same when you touch these objects? Are not some 
objects lighter than others?
The objects, we use, are made up of certain materials (such as 
paper, wood, cloth, glass, cotton etc.). For example, the notebook is 
made up of paper. The notebook is the object and paper is the material.
The substance from which an object is made is called a material.

leaves, garlic, mustard oil etc. in separate containers. She keeps all the 
containers containing spices together. Different containers containing 
different dals (e.g. lentils) are also kept together. As a result she easily 
gets what she needs.

1 Activity 5.3:
Write the names of materials known to you that are used to make a

 Your mother cooks curries in a kerahi (pan). The kerahi is made 
up of metal. Hollow bamboo segment is also used to cook rice and curry. 
But can you always cook rice in the same bamboo segment? Surely not; 
it will burn. Do you chop fruits and vegetables? The knife used for 
chopping is usually made up of iron. Can the knife be made from wood 
or bamboo?
 The metal pan does not burn even if it is used repeatedly for 
cooking.  This is the property of metal. On the other hand, the hollow 
bamboo segment burns. That is also property of bamboo. The iron knife 
is quite hard. While a bamboo knife is not so. These are the properties 
of iron and bamboo.

 What will happen if tumblers are made up of paper or cloth? In

 How to choose the material needed to make an object? You choose

5.2 Different properties of materials 
 Let us learn about some of the properties of materials.
5.2.1  External Appearance
 Have you seen a fresh nail? Again, have you  noticed the sharp 
side of a knife? The nail and the knife are made of iron. Kettles and 
saucepans are generally used for heating water. These are usually made 
of aluminium. Hence, you have come to know that iron and aluminium 
look different; i.e. iron and aluminium differ in appearnce. Similarly, 
copper has different external appearance; it is deep brown in colour. 
Wood and bamboo also have different external appearances.
 Sometimes, more than one type of materials are used to make an 
object. For example, metal and plastic are used to make a pen. 
 Look at Fig. 5.5. Classify the objects shown in the figure in 
different ways. You can  consider properties, such as colour, shape etc. 
 Hence, we come to know that objects or materials can be classified 
according to their properties.

5.3.2 Hard and Soft material
 Some materials are very hard,  for example: iron. Iron is difficult 
to compress when you press by using hand. But the eraser that you use, 
can be easily compressed by using your hand. So, the eraser is made of 
soft material. 
 You cannot test everything by presssing it with your hands. In 
such cases, we can examine with a metal key. Some items can easily be 
scratched with a metal key, while the others cannot. Materials that can 
be easily pressed or scratched with a key are considered to be soft. On 
the other hand, materials that cannot be pressed or is difficult to scratch 
easily, is a hard material. These properties, however, are relative. For 
example, wood is harder than rubber but softer than iron.

5.2.4  Water-soluble and insoluble materials  
 In summer you surely drink ' sarbat'. Do you know how is it 
prepared? Take water in a glass and add a teaspoon of sugar and a little 
salt. Add a little lemon juice and stir well with the spoon. What do you 
observe? The crystals of sugar and salt gradually become smaller and 
smaller and eventually disappear. However, the sweet taste of sugar 
comes into the sarbat. The taste of salt will also be there. Although 
sugar and salt are present in the water; but they cannot be seen. The 
water remains transparent. We say that sugar and salt get dissolved in 
water meaning sugar and salt are soluble in water.

5.3.7. Volume
 Every object occupies some space. Just look at the objects in 
your house. The boxes, cupboards, cricket bats, balls etc. in your house  
occupies some space, does it not? The bag that you bring to school 
also occupies some space. Therefore, if you keep your bag on the 
bench, there will be limitation of space able to sit on it. Similarly, your 
classroom or house occupies  some space. The house certainly takes up 
more space than the classroom, right? The volume of an object is the 
space occupied by it. 
 Why did the water overflow when the lemon was dropped in the 
first tumbler? This is because the lemon occupies some of the spaces 
inside the glass. The space occupied by the lemon is its volume.
Do you know ?
Sometimes in common language weight is used for mass as it is 
determined by weighting. You will learn more about mass and weight 
and their relation in higher classes.

5.3.8 What is matter? 
 Now you know that water, sand and pebbles have mass. Each of 
them occupies some space, meaning they have volume. In fact, every 
substance has mass and volume. Anything that has mass and volume is 
matter.
 Mass refers to the amount of matter. That is the mass of an object 
is the amount of matter in the object. It is generally expressed in gram 
(g) and kilogram (kg) units.
 Anything that occupies space and has mass is matter or anything 
which has mass and volume is matter.

 Take a glass tumbler, a large bowl (charia), a piece of paper 
and  water. Dry the tumbler properly. Paste the piece of paper at 
inside bottom of the tumbler using gum. Fill the bowl with water. 
Turn the tumbler upside down and gently press it into the water.

paper is not wet.

tumbler, which appears empty, was actually full with air. Since air 
occupies the space inside the tumbler, water could not reach the 
paper.

 We have learnt that the objects around us consist of materials. A 
material is a type of matter. Different materials look different and their 
properties are also different. Some are hard while others are soft. We 
can see through some objects; but we cannot see through some other 
objects. Some are soluble in water, while some others are not. These 
properties   help in classification of objects based on their properties.
 Now inflate the football and place it on the left pan of balance. 
Does the pointer still indicate zero? Certainly not. To balance it, more 
sand has to be put on the right pan [Fig 5.15 (b)]. This means that mass 
of the inflated football is more than that of the deflated football. Hence 
we come to know that air has mass. Thus, air has mass and it occupies 
space. Therefore, air is a matter.

 Let us have a look at the materials around us. Most of these are 
visible to our naked eyes ; e.g. water, soil, sand, metals, plastics, food 
items, clothes etc. Some others are invisible ; e.g, air. All these materials 
are called matter in science. Matter may be of three types – solid, liquid 
and gas. There are sugar, salt, rice, dal, tea leaves etc. in your house. 
These are solid matters (or simply solid). Water, milk, oil etc. form 
liquids. Air is of course gaseous matter.
6.1 Matter, substance and mixture
 Some of these matters consist of only one type of substance. For 
example, a piece of iron consists of iron only. Similarly, a glass of pure 
water consists of water only, and nothing else. Some others consist of 
more than one type of matter ; e.g. soil and air. Matter may be either a 
pure matter (substance) or a mixture. Now let us try to understand what 
substance and mixture are.
	 Take 	 a	 glass	 bottle	 and	 half	 fill	 it	 with	 water.	 Now	 put	 some	
sandy soil into it and stir thoroughly with a spoon. Then allow it to 
stand undisturbed for some time. You will see three distinct layers in 
the bottle as shown in the Fig. 6.1. These are the three components 
present in the soil. The top layer is formed by clay with water, the 
middle layer consists of sand while the bottom layer consists of pebbles 
(small stones). We may call each of these components a substance. Soil 
is a mixture of these substances. A substance consists of only one type 
of matter. But a mixture consists of more than one type of substances. 
Each substance in a mixture is a component of the mixture.

6.2 Why do we need separation of substances of a mixture?
Will you be able to eat chira	 (flattened	 rice)	 if	 husks	 are	 not	
removed from it ? Certainly not. What will be the consequence if small 
pebbles, generally mixed with masoor dal (lentil) or rice, are not these 
removed before cooking ? Thus, in our daily life, we see that some less 
useful materials are there with the more useful materials. Before using, 
we need to separate the components. Thus, separation of substances is 
necessary.
It is not that separation is necessary in case of food items only. 
Separation is mainly done for three purposes.
	 ¿	 To remove non-useful components :  In water treatment  
plants, insoluble impurities and microorganisms are removed 
from water to make it potable.
	 ¿ 	To obtain useful product : Sea water is evaporated to obtain 
common salt. Salt is used extensively in our kitchens and 
industries.
	 ¿	 To obtain pure material : Pure sugar crystals are obtained from 
sugarcane juice, whereas the impurities remain in the juice.
6.3 Methods of separation
Now, we will explore how we can separate substances from a 
mixture. In order to separate substances present in a mixture we need to 
know the characteristics of the components. A particular characteristic 
of	one	of	the	components	is	used.	This	may	be	difference	in	size,	shape,	
colour, weight, physical state, water soluble or not, attracted by magnet 
or not etc. The substance that needs to be separated from a mixture 
should not have the same characteristic with those present in the other 
components.

6.3.2 Sieving 
 Sometimes a stock of rice grains may contain some amount of 
paddy seeds (dhan). Have you seen how paddy seeds are separated 
from the rice grains? Sometimes it is done by handpicking, isn’t it? 
But, if the quantity of seed is high, then what does she do? She uses a 
bamboo sieve to separate the rice grains [Fig. 6.3 (a)]. The seeds, being 
bigger	in	size	than	rice	grains,	remain	on	the	sieve.	The	rice	grains	pass	
through	the	holes	of	the	sieve.	Again,	during	preparation	of	rice	flour	
in a ‘dheki’ or grinder, another sieve is used [Fig 6.3(b) ]. The holes of 
this	sieve	are	very	small.	The	fine	particles	of	rice	grains	pass	through	
the holes of the sieve. Separation of the components of a mixture using 
sieve is termed as sieving.
 The same technique is used at construction sites to separate 
pebbles from sand. The stones present in the sand remain on the sieve 
and the sand particle passes through the holes [Fig. 6.3(c)].

6.3.3 Threshing  
You know that farmers work hard to produce food crops for us. 
They cultivate and harvest the stalks bearing the matured seeds. Then 
they separate the seeds from the stalks. You must have seen bundles of 
paddy	stalks	lying	in	the	paddy	fields	after	harvesting.	The	stalks	are	
sun dried before the seeds are separated from them. Each stalk carries 
many seeds. Imagine the number of seeds in hundreds of bundles of 
such stalks! How does the farmer separate the seeds from the stalks?
 You may pluck mangoes or guavas from the trees. But seeds of 
various types of crops such as paddy, pulses, mustard, wheat etc are 
much smaller than mangoes or guavas. So, plucking them from their 
stalks takes lots of time. The process that is used to separate seeds 
from stalks etc. is called threshing. It is the process of beating out the 
seeds from the harvested crop plants. Perhaps you have seen threshing 
of paddy seeds from the stalks using bullocks [ ‘morona mora’, Fig. 
6.4(a)]. Threshing is also done by stomping the paddy stalks especially 
in the rainy season. Sometimes the stalks are beaten to separate the 
seeds from the stalk. Nowadays machines are used to thresh out large 
quantities of harvested seeds from the crop plants. These machines are 
called threshers.

6.3.4 Winnowing 
The seeds obtained after threshing may contain some small cut 
pieces of leaves, unwanted light debrises and immature seeds. These 
unwanted components must be removed from the seeds, isn’t it? This 
is done by winnowing. This method involves separating the heavier 
components from the lighter ones with the help of wind. Just consider 
one	example.	Y ou	definitely	like	to	eat	roasted	peanuts.	Take	some	of	
them and rub between your palms. You will see the red skins being 
separated from the white peanuts. Now blow air on the mixture from 
your	mouth.	What	do	you	see?	The	red	skins,	being	lighter,	fly	away	
and the tasty peanuts remain exposed. Samething is done in winnowing. 
After threshing, the seeds are taken on a bamboo tray (‘kula’) 
for winnowing [Fig.6.5(a)]. But separating large quantities of grains 
by winnowing with bamboo tray is laborious and time consuming. 
So winnowing is done by another technique. The farmer stands on an 
elevated platform, in an open space. Then he slowly slides the mixture of 
seeds and small fragments of stalks. Seeds, being heavier, fall straight to 
the ground. The broken fragments of leaves, immature seeds, fragments 
of stalks and dust and sand particles are lighter. These fall at a little 
distance away as these are carried away by wind. Thus, pure seeds are 
obtained [Fig.6.5(b)].
Have	 you	 seen	 separating	 husks	 from	 flattened	 rice	 (chira) by 
winnowing by using a bamboo tray?

6.4 Sedimentation and Decantation 
Have you seen ever your mother washing rice grains with water 
before cooking it? She rubs the rice grains with water in a pot. Some 
impurities	 in	 the	 form	 of	 light	 particles	 float	 in	 the	 water.	 Some	 get	
mixed with water, making the water turbid. The rice grains being heavy 
settle at the bottom of the pot. Then she slowly tills the pot carefully and 
allows the water to drain away. The impurities are also drained away 
along with the water. But the rice grains remain in the pot. 
While preparing tea, generally a strainer is used to separate the 
tea leaves. If you do not have a strainer, what will you do ? Just allow 
the wet tea leaves to settle down at the bottom of the pot. Then slowly 
incline the pot holding it above another pot to transfer the supernatant 
tea. While doing this, do not jerk the pot so as to prevent the tea leaves 
from falling into the pot below. This is a very simple method, is not it ? 
Here, the tea leaves, settled at the bottom is the sediment. This process 
of separating liquid (i.e., tea) from solid (i.e. tea leaves) by removing 
the liquid part from the sediment is called decantation.

slowly. What happens? Do both the components (sand and powdered 
leaves) fall at the same place? Is there a component that is blown 
away? Did the wind help to separate these two components ?

 In the above examples of rice grain and water as well as tea leaves 
and water, each one contains a solid in a liquid medium. Separation of 
these mixtures has two steps. Initially the mixture is allowed to stand 
for sometime without shaking it. The heavy substance such as rice 
grains or tea leaves settle down. The matter that settles at the bottom 
of a liquid layer is called the sediment. The process of settling down 
of heavier insoluble particles  at the bottom of a liquid layer is called 
sedimentation.
1 Activity 6.3: 
Materials required : Two beakers (or glass tumbler), one glass 
rod or spoon, water and sand.
Take a mixture of water and sand in a beaker. Stir it well using 
a glass rod. The mixture will be turbid. Now leave it undisturbed for 
some time. What do you see? Sand settles down at the bottom of the 
beaker because it is heavy. This is called sedimentation. The sand 
in this case is the sediment. [Fig. 6.7(a)]. Then pour the clear water 
layer	to	the	other	beaker	in	such	a	way	that	the	sand	does	not	flow	
down along with it. The clear water collected is called decant. By 
using this method, you have separated insoluble sand (solid) from 
water (liquid)  as shown in Fig. 6.7(b).

6.5 Filtration 
Is decantation a perfect process of separation ? There is always a 
chance of a small amount of solid (e.g. sand) getting mixed with water. 
Similarly, during decantation of tea, some tea leaves may remain in the 
tea. Then how can we solve this problem ?
 The same principle is used for separating a mixture of two liquids 
that do not mix with each other. For example, oil and water don’t mix 
with each other. On shaking they form white turbidity. If the mixture 
of such liquids is allowed to stand for sometime, they form two layers 
(Fig. 6.8). The oil that forms the top layer can then be separated from 
the lower water layer by decantation.

   salt-water 
	 A 	mixture	of	water	and	salt	cannot	be	separated	by	filtration.	This	
is because the salt particles in water are too small and are soluble in 
water.	They	can	pass	through	the	fine	holes	of	the	filter	cloth.	Salt	in	
water can be separated by boiling salt water until the whole amount of 
water is evaporated. But salt particles don’t evaporate. Separation of 
a miscible substance from a liquid by evaporating the liquid is called 
evaporation. For example, when the mixture of water and salt in the tin-
can was heated for some time, whole amount of  the water evaporated 
as water vapour and salt was left behind.

Fig 6.14: Obtaining salt from sea water
Where does the common salt come from ?
Can you think of curry, 
fried food etc. without 
salt ? Certainly not. 
Common salt is a very 
essential commodity 
for all of us. But 
how does salt reach 
our homes ? Firstly, 
it is extracted from 
sea water. Sea water 
contains many other 
substances along with 
common salt. When sea water is allowed to stand in shallow pits, water 
slowly evaporates. After a few days, the water evaporates completely 
leaving behind the common salt mixed with some other substances 
(Fig. 6.14). Common salt is then obtained from this mixture through a 
process called purification.

inside the pot, the fat portion comes 
up to the upper part of the pot. This 
fat is called cream. The process is 
called churning of milk or curd. 
Traditionally cream is separated 
from milk in this way (Fig. 6.15)

Magnetic separation 
Materials required - Sand, iron filings, magnet and a piece of paper.
Fig. 6.16 : Separation of 
magnetic materials from sand
Fig. 6.17 : Lifting of heavy magnetic materials in industries 
from other materials
Sand	+	iron	filling
Magnet
Sand
Iron 
filling
 Take a mixture of sand and iron 
filings	on	a	piece	of	paper.	Now	bring	
a magnet near to this mixture. What 
do	 you	 observe?	 Iron	 filings	 cling	 to	
the magnet and hence get separated. 
Collect	 the	 iron	 filings	 in	 a	 piece	 of	
paper. Repeat this activity till all the 
iron	 filings	 are	 separated	 from	 the	
sand. Sand will remain on the paper. 
Iron is attracted by magnet. So iron is 
called a magnetic substance. But sand 
is not attracted by magnet and so it is a 
non-magnetic substance. This method 
of separation of magnetic substances 
from non-magnetic materials using 
a magnet is known as magnetic 
separation.
 In industries, iron pieces are 
separated from other materials by this 
method (Fig.6.17).

  Separation methods  Hand picking, Threshing

What you have learnt ?
	¿	Matter can be a pure substance or a mixture of substances.
	¿	Substances can be separated from a mixture.
	¿	A mixture has characters of its constituents, on the basis of 
which, they are separated. 
	¿	The separation of components of a mixture is done to remove 
unwanted constituents, and to obtain useful and pure substance.
	¿	Hand picking is used to separate solid substances when their 
sizes	are	sufficiently	large.
	¿	Sieving can be used for separating larger and smaller solid 
substances in a mixture.
	¿	If mixtures have light and heavy solid substances, winnowing 
can be used for separation. 
	¿	An insoluble substance in a liquid can be separated by 
sedimentation and decantation.
	¿	Filtration is used to separate an insoluble solid substance from 
a liquid.
	¿	Evaporation is used to separate a soluble  solid substance from 
a liquid.
	¿	Magnetic substances can be separated from a non-magnetic 
substance by using a magnet.
	¿	More than one method of separation can be used to separate 
the components of mixtures with multiple components.
	¿	Some of the separation technique are traditionally practiced in 
our	 society.	 These	 are-	 Preparing	 tea;	 traditional	 water	 filter	
using sand; stone and charcoal; threshing paddy seeds using 
feet and bullocks; winnowing; use of ‘ dheki’ ‘and sieve for 
making	rice	flour,	making	sugar	and	molasses	from	sugarcane	
juice; separating husk from wet ‘moong dal’; churning of milk; 
making cottage cheese (paneer) from milk; collecting salt from 
sea water etc.

1. Group Activity : Separation of substances using multiple 
processes
If a mixture has only two substances as components then a sin-
gle	method	is	sufficient	to	separate	the	substances	from	the	mixture.	
However, if the mixture has more than two components, then what 
will you do? 
Consider the Fig. 6.1 given at the very beginning of this chapter. 
Can you separate the three layers of clay(with water), sand and pebbles 
present in the tumbler by handpicking?  No, because there is water 
in this mixture. Water cannot be separated by handpicking, because 
you	cannot	pick	water	by	your	fingers.	Can	you	use	winnowing?	No	
because wind cannot separate these three components. Can we think 
of sieving directly in this case? Still no, since the wet mixture cannot 
be sieved. So let us try to collect the components in pure form by 
designing a procedure. This will require involvement of the methods 
of separation discussed in this chapter. 
What do you observe in the container of soil-water mixture? 
Y ou	will	find	that	the	sand	and	pebble	settle	down	at	the	bottom	of	
the  tumbler as these are heavier. This is sedimentation. Sand par-
ticles are smaller than the pebbles and they are light. So, the clay 
portion is in the top layer mixed with water. Try to transfer the top 
layer to another container very carefully inclining the tip of the con-
tainer. See that the sediments are not disturbed and remains in the 
first	container.	This	process	is	decantation.  Thus clay (with water) 
gets separated from the sediment (sand + pebbles). 
The clay from the clay-water mixture can be separated in three 
ways. Firstly, keep the mixture undisturbed for one or two days.  The 
clay will settle at bottom of the pot. This is sedimentation. Water is 
separated it by decantation and the clay will remain in the pot. Sec-
ondly,	filter	the	clay-water	mixture	directly	using	a	cloth	to	separate	
the clay from water. This is filtration. Thirdly, boil the clay-water 
mixture until water evaporates completely leaving the clay. This is 
evaporation.
Now the only sand-pebble mixture remains. Dry the mixture 
in the Sun. It will remove any residual water. You can hand pick 
the	pebbles.	But	it	may	not	be	so	effective.	Sieve	the	mixture	using	
a household  sieve. This is sieving. This will separate sand from the 
pebbles.

Elements of weather Instruments used to measure
Air temperature Thermometer (Maximum and Minimum 
temperature)
Amount of rainfall Rain gauge
Direction of wind Wind vane
Speed of air Anemometer

 Data for rainfall may not be recorded everyday as there may not 
be rain always. If you get rains, you can record it. From the table you 
can easily understand that the maximum and minimum temperature, 
humidity, amount of rainfall may not be same in all the seven days 
of a week. Perhaps the maximum and minimum temperature recorded 
may or may not be the same for some days. You will surely get such 
differences.
 Temperature and humidity of the atmosphere may change every 
day. Hence the weather of a place may change every day or every 
week. This is called the change of weather. Weather is such a complex 
phenomenon that it may change within a  very short period of time. 
Have we not experienced of getting storm, rainfall, lightning suddenly? 
We are astonished when heavy rainfall vanishes within a very short 
time followed by bright sunshine. 
 Now we have understood that the temporary and local conditions 
of the atmosphere at a specific place and time, including temperature, 
humidity rainfall etc. is called the weather of the place of that time. 
Temperature, humidity and other factors are called elements of weather.
 Do you know what instruments are used by the meteorologist 
in the meteorological centre to collect data about the factors of 
weather? Usually they use the instruments given in the following 
table.
 You must have heard your elders or grandparents telling about the 
present days getting changed in climate and about higher temperature 
in present days then the days before. What is this ‘climate’ your elders 
or grandparents are talking about?

7.2 Climate 
 Try to recall, what you have learnt about the weather of a place 
for each day of a week by collecting the data of the factors of weather 
like temperature, humidity, rainfall etc.? We shall be able to find out the 
average of maximum and minimum temperature for seven days. It is 
also possible to find out the average weather of a  particular region for a 
long period. The average weather pattern of a place over a long period 
of time, say 25-30 years or more  is called the climate of that place. 
The mean records of weather for several decades help to determine the 
climate of a place. It means that records of the factors of weather for 
several decades help us to determine the climate of a place. Take an 
example, suppose the average temperature of a place for a period 25-30 
of years is high, then we can say that the climate of that place is hot. If 
the average rainfall is also high, then we can say that the place is hot 
and damp.
       Fig. 7.1 : Picture of desert with camel
 You have surely heard about the climate of a desert which  is hot 
and dry. It means the temperature of a desert is high for many years and 
the region also receives very less rainfall over a long period of time. 
The scientists of the meteorological department collect the information 
of weather of each day and preserve this for several decades. This 
preserved information of a place is used to determine the climate of that 
place. Means of temperature, humidity, rainfall of a place are worked 
out. Let us learn how to calculate the mean temperature of a place. First 
we find out the average of the temperature of each month of a year. 
Secondly, we calculate average of such average temperature for many 
years. This gives the mean temperature of that place. Is the atmospheric 
temperature same in all the regions of the Earth? Let us discuss.

7.3 Climatic regions of the earth
 Do you know that light of the sun does not fall equally on all 
regions of the earth? The sun does not even set at the poles of the  Earth 
for six months and does not rise for another six months. That means 
the sun only rises and falls once in a year in the poles. Polar regions are 
very cold. These regions are covered with snow.  
 Tropical region is situated in the middle of the earth. This region 
lies between Tropic of Cancer approximately in the North of the equator 
and Tropic of Capricon in the south of the equator. Most of the heat from 
the sun falls in these regions. So these regions get plenty of rainfall and 
have high temperature. North temperate climatic region is situated in 
the North of the tropical region and South temperate climatic region is 
situated in the south of the tropical region. The climate of the temperate 
region is neither hot nor cold. Seasons like summer, autumn, winter, 
spring are seen in these region.
 You must have learnt that variation in weather and climate 
occur due to the sun. You will learn about effect of climate on soil and 
organisms elaborately in higher classes. Climate influences the dress, 
food habit, habitation, livelihood, health etc. of human being. Hence 
the shape, size and structure of plants and animals living in different 
regions are found to be different.
 Climate of a region in the earth also depends upon its height from 
sea level, shape of the land and distance of the place from sea. For these 
reasons differences in climate of different regions of India are found. 
For example, the desert of Rajasthan is very hot compared to very cold 
climate of Jammu and Kashmir.

7.4 Climate of Assam : Its impact on agriculture and daily life 
Assam and North-eastern region receive very heavy rains. The 
humidity of air in this region is high. Due to tropical monsoon, Assam 
experiences neither very hot nor very cold climate. Therefore, the climate 
of Assam is generally ‘tropical monsoon rainfall’ type. The people of 
this region also enjoy the change of seasons as in the temperate climatic 
region. 
 You know that the growth of all plants depends on sunlight, 
water and soil. Therefore, agriculture in any place depends on the 
weather, climate and soil of that place. The air pressure, temperature 
and rainfall vary in different seasons like summer, rainy season, autumn 
and winter. Different types of crops are grown in different seasons 
accordingly. Assam also grows different crops according to the seasons. 
During the summer and rainy season, Assam receives heavy rains due 
to southwest monsoon winds. The air temperature is also higher during 
this time. This weather is suitable for paddy, jute etc. Hence these crops 
are grown in Assam. These are called Kharif crops. Similarly, Rabi 
crops like wheat, maize and mustard are grown in the early autumn 
and winter season (dry season). Vegetables like potatoes, spinach 
etc. are usually grown in winter as they require less heat and water. 
Thus, there is a good relationship between climate and agriculture.

¿ The weather of a place is the daily condition in the 
 atmosphere caused by atmospheric temperature, humidity,  
 rainfall, wind speed etc. 
¿ Component of weather includes atmospheric temperature,  
 humidity and wind direction and  speed.
¿ The weather changes everyday or every week i.e. frequently. 
¿ The climate of a place is determined from the long term (25- 
 30 years)  average weather conditions. 
¿ All changes of weather are affected by the Sun. In the polar  
 region, effect of winter is there throughout the year. Sun does  
 not set for six months of the year and does not rise for the  
 remaining six months in the polar region. 
¿ Climate is the long-term pattern of weather conditions in any  
 region.
¿ Climate change affects every aspect of our lives.
¿ Everyone must be aware of the problems  that can be caused  
 by climate change and try to mitigate impacts of climate   
 change through life style and activities.
